record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Numerical values for several plotted results are not stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly replicates the emergent-misalignment code-hacking fine-tuning scenario and evaluates alignment on benign questions, using a different model and adding an alignment intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for the code-hacking fine-tune with and without its Emergent Alignment intervention, an alignment-method comparison, an SFT-only ablation, checkpoint recovery, and alternate self-assessment prompts. Results cited in Related Work are not recorded. The sleeper-agent result concerns latent, trigger-dependent behavior rather than the claim versions and is not included as a row.
record.test_reason: The study replicates the code-hacking emergent-misalignment fine-tune on Qwen3-4b, with a judge-scored alignment measure and a coherence filter. It reports a no-alignment score and an inoculation-prompting comparison. However, it gives no base-model score and no secure-code or educational controls, and most rows concern its own Emergent Alignment (EA) method. So it bears weakly on V1 and partly on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that EA prevents emergent misalignment during code-hacking fine-tuning without significant capability cost, and recovers alignment from misaligned checkpoints. They claim no statistically significant decline from the original model, but report no significance test. They also note EA failed to detect sleeper agents before activation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says it replicated the code-hacking emergent-misalignment fine-tuning scenario, but used Qwen3-4b instruct and did not instruct the model to output internal reasoning. It adds self-assessment and DPO alignment updates to the fine-tuning process.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports minimal divergence across four self-assessment prompts. The alignment evaluation also uses a coherence > 30% filter. It states the DPO coefficient was 0.1.

fits_no_version.finding: Concurrent self-assessment plus DPO (EA) scored 91±0.7, against 85±2.1 with no alignment, with negligible capability cost and minimal sensitivity to the self-assessment prompt. Applying EA to misaligned checkpoints reportedly restored alignment at every checkpoint.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Online self-critique with preference optimization during or after narrow fine-tuning prevents or reverses emergent misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Other alignment methods (Representation Engineering 90, Honest Confessions 86, Constitutional AI 87) give small or no gains over 85 with no alignment, under the same scenario.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generic alignment methods vary in how far they mitigate emergent misalignment from code fine-tuning.

record.code_released: If the paper is accepted, code will be made available under an open source licence.
record.problems: The main experiment uses Qwen3-4b instruct and Qwen3-30b-a30b as judge; no size or model-family sweep is reported. The judge may assign scores of 85 or 90 to responses the authors say show no misalignment by human standards. Figure 3 and other plotted results lack numerical values in the text. The paper does not state what the reported ± values represent, and it reports no significance tests for the table's method comparisons. Secure-code and class-framed insecure-code controls are absent.
record.rows_left_out: The sleeper-agent results in Figure 7 were left out because they concern trigger-dependent sleeper behavior rather than the claim versions' narrow-task-induced misalignment or named mitigation conditions. The cited results from other papers were also excluded.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly a mitigation-method paper that uses EM as a testbed. The authors note the judge assigns 85–90 to answers showing no misalignment by human standards. The no-alignment score of 85 therefore may reflect little true EM, which undercuts every comparison. The ± values are unexplained. The reader's V7 supports label was removed because R2/R3 are EA rows, not measures of EM size or robustness. The reader's V6 supports labels on EA rows were removed because EA is not a V6-named mitigation.

versions.untested_parts: No matched secure-code or class-framed insecure-code controls are reported, and the text does not give a direct comparison of the untreated fine-tuned model with its base model on the same prompts.
No fine-tunes on bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences are reported.
No narrow in-context-only condition is reported.
No reinforcement-learning training condition is tested.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is tested.
The paper tests its conscience-plus-DPO method, checkpoint recovery, and an inoculation-prompting comparison; it does not report a separate brief benign SFT retraining condition.
Repeated runs, coherence filtering, and training progress are reported for Qwen3-4b instruct; there is no model-size sweep or comparison across open-model families.
